newsitem.title: USA: Iraq unlikely to act against U.S. now -- Albright.
newsitem.headline: Iraq unlikely to act against U.S. now -- Albright.

text.p: Iraqi President Saddam Hussein seems unlikely to provoke a renewed attack by newly strengthened U.S. forces, and the United States will not be pressed into "overreacting," the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations said on Sunday.
"We are not going to be pressed into overreacting," Madeleine Albright said on the NBC program "Meet the Press." "It looks as though Saddam Hussein is not going to do anything else."

In an apparent effort to head off U.S. preparations for a fresh punitive strike, Iraq said on Friday it would no longer fire antiaircraft missiles at U.S. and allied warplanes enforcing "no fly" zones in northern and southern Iraq.

On Sunday, the Pentagon delayed plans for the possible deployment of up to 5,000 additional Army troops to join a U.S. buildup in and around the Gulf, apparently because of Kuwaiti qualms about being host to them.

"Because the situation is ever-changing, it seems they may or may not ever be utilized," said Navy Lt. Cmdr. Scott Campbell, a Pentagon spokesman. The troops from Fort Hood in Texas had been alerted on Friday night for possible deployment to the Gulf on Sunday.

As part of the buildup, the Pentagon ordered a second aircraft carrier to the region, sent F-117A Stealth bombers to Kuwait and transferred B-52 bombers to the British base at Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean Island.
Defense Secretary William Perry, shuttling between Gulf allies and Turkey to consult on Iraq policy, left open on Sunday the possibility of fresh strikes against Iraq.
Asked if more U.S. strikes against Iraq were still possible, Perry told a news conference on a brief visit to Kuwait: "Yes, it is still a possibility."

The United States "will take whatever action is necessary" to enforce an expanded southern Iraqi no-fly zone up to the 33rd parallel, which runs 30 miles (50 km) south of Baghdad, and to protect the pilots who patrol it, he said.
Albright said the United States would remain "resolute" in its effort to prevent Saddam, who invaded Kuwait in 1990, from threatening its neighbors again.
"Basically, we have built up our forces there," she said. "They've acted as a very strong deterrent. We will be resolute."

Pressed on whether it would take another provocation for the United States to renew the attacks it unleashed this month after an Iraqi-backed onslaught on one Kurdish faction, Albright said: "I think we're going to keep watching the whole issue very, very carefully."

"We want to make sure that our pilots are safe and that the no-fly zone is something that we can maintain," she added. The United States and its allies set up "no-fly" zones in Iraq's north and south after the 1991 Gulf War.
Republicans kept up their attacks on President Bill Clinton's Iraq policy, faulting it for splitting the alliance that drove Saddam from Kuwait in the Gulf War.

"I am not sure exactly what we are accomplishing. We still have not heard what's the mission, what is success. What is the purpose," House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said on "Meet the Press."

"If it is to protect the Kurds, it has failed, if it is to protect Kuwaitis, they don't need protection. So we are spending a lot of money and risking some Americans that I am not sure what the game is," Gingrich said.
In Kuwait, Perry dismissed the pledge by Baghdad to abandon attacks on planes patrolling the Western-imposed zones, saying: "We cannot rely on Saddam Hussein's promises."

The latest crisis between the United States and Iraq began on Aug. 31 when Saddam's forces surged into a Kurdish enclave in northern Iraq and helped a faction seize the city of Arbil and rout a rival group. The crisis deepened after Iraqi forces fired one or more surface-to-air missiles at U.S. warplanes patrolling the no-fly zones.

Washington punished Iraq for intervening in the factional fighting in its Kurdish north by launching 44 cruise missiles at air defense systems in southern Iraq. With Britain's support, the United States also expanded the no-flight zone northward to the outskirts of Baghdad.
